passages.t: A ruler from Bethlehem, and peace
passages.happening:
Jerusalem is under siege, and the judge of Israel is struck on the cheek with a rod (verse 1). ‘But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are small among the clans of Judah, out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel’ (verse 2), one whose origins are from long ago, from ancient days.

So Israel will be given up until she who is in labor has given birth, and then the rest of his brothers will return (verse 3). ‘He will stand and shepherd His flock in the strength of the LORD, in the majestic name of the LORD His God’ (verse 4), and they will live securely, for his greatness will reach to the ends of the earth. ‘And He will be our peace when Assyria invades our land’ (verse 5). Seven shepherds, even eight, will be raised against it, and he will deliver them (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
Micah's world was dominated by Assyria. Samaria fell in 722 BC, and in 701 BC Sennacherib invaded Judah and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem. The siege and the Assyrian invasion fit that world closely, though some interpreters hear a later siege, the Babylonian one of 587 or 586 BC, in verse 1. In the Hebrew Bible the BSB's 5:1 is 4:14, so 5:2 is 5:1.

Bethlehem Ephrathah was a small farming town about six miles south of Jerusalem. Ephrathah was an older name for the area or its clan, and the double name sets this Bethlehem apart from another town of the same name. Its only importance was its history: it was David's hometown, where Samuel anointed the shepherd boy. To say the ruler would come from Bethlehem rather than Jerusalem was to say that God would begin the royal line again from its humble start. The word for clans also means thousand, a tribal or military unit; Bethlehem was too small to count among them.

The ruler's origins are from of old, from ancient days. Elsewhere in Micah and Amos these words mean the distant past, the age of the patriarchs or David, which is why most modern commentators read the line as the ruler's ancient roots in David's line. Many Christian interpreters, from the church fathers onward, read it as pointing beyond human ancestry. Kings were often called shepherds of their people, and seven, even eight is a way of saying more than enough.
passages.later: God sent Samuel to Jesse of Bethlehem to anoint a king from among his sons (1 Samuel 16:1). When Herod asked where the Christ was to be born, the chief priests and scribes answered, ‘In Bethlehem in Judea’ (Matthew 2:5), and quoted this verse in a form that ends, ‘who will be the shepherd of My people Israel’ (Matthew 2:6). John records that people expected the Christ ‘from Bethlehem, the village where David lived’ (John 7:42).
passages.hard:
Since no ruler from Bethlehem defeated Assyria in Micah's day, did the promise fail?

Readers answer in several ways. Some see a near fulfillment in Hezekiah's rescue from Sennacherib in 701 BC, with the Bethlehem ruler as a fuller figure beyond it. Others note that Assyria in verses 5 and 6 stands for the great oppressor of the day, so the promise is that God's king will overcome whatever empire threatens his people. Still others read the chapter as one picture of God's future, in which Micah could only describe final victory with the enemies he knew.

What the text itself makes clear is that the ruler's greatness will reach to the ends of the earth, far beyond any eighth-century event. Christians confess that the promise meets its fullness in Jesus, as Matthew says, while recognizing that Micah spoke first to people who feared the Assyrian army at the gates. Matthew's wording differs from the Hebrew: where Micah calls Bethlehem small, Matthew says it is by no means least, reading the promise from its fulfillment, and his last line draws on God's charge to David (2 Samuel 5:2).
passages.asks: God chose the smallest town for his greatest ruler. Ask where you have assumed that what is small does not matter to God. And this ruler will be his people's peace. Ask what it would mean for him to be your peace when you feel besieged.

passages.t: Dew and lion, and what God will cut away
passages.happening:
The remnant of Jacob will be among many peoples ‘like dew from the LORD, like showers on the grass’ (verse 7), which wait for no one. It will also be among the nations like a lion among the animals of the forest (verse 8), and its enemies will be cut off (verse 9).

Then God says what he will remove from his own people. ‘In that day,’ declares the LORD, he will remove their horses and wreck their chariots (verse 10). He will take away their cities and tear down their strongholds (verse 11). He will cut off their sorceries and fortune-tellers (verse 12), their carved images and sacred pillars, ‘so that you will no longer bow down to the work of your own hands’ (verse 13). He will root out the Asherah poles (verse 14), and take vengeance on the nations that have not obeyed him (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Dew in a dry land was a gift that came without human effort, and a lion among sheep was the picture of unstoppable power. The remnant of Jacob is described with both, side by side, each with the same opening line. It will be a gift that comes from God and a strength no one can stop.

The list in verses 10 to 14 names what Judah had trusted: horses and chariots brought in for war, fortified cities, fortune-tellers, carved images, standing stones, and Asherah poles, the wooden objects linked with the Canaanite goddess Asherah. The repeated verb, cut off, falls like a hammer. It is a cleansing aimed first at God's own people, and only in the last verse at the disobedient nations.

God's peace does not come through horses and walls. He takes away what his people trusted instead of him, so that they will trust him alone. The lion picture belongs to the language of that age. It is no warrant for violence by anyone, and it makes no claim about any nation or conflict today.
passages.later: The law warned Israel's king not to multiply horses (Deuteronomy 17:16), and a psalm says, ‘Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God’ (Psalm 20:7).
passages.asks: God promises to take away the horses, walls and idols his people leaned on. Ask what you lean on instead of God. And ask whether you would welcome him cutting it away, if it meant trusting him alone.
